# A mouse in the elevated plus maze {#sec-movement-mouse}

In this case study, we'll use the [`movement` package](https://movement.neuroinformatics.dev/) to analyse a mouse navigating an [elevated plus maze (EPM)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elevated_plus_maze)—a widely used behavioural assay for measuring anxiety in rodents. Our end goal is to quantify how much time the mouse spends in each region of the maze.

Before you get started, make sure you've set up the `animals-in-motion-env` environment (refer to [prerequisites @sec-install-movement]) and are using it to run this code.

## The elevated plus maze

The EPM consists of two open arms and two closed arms (enclosed by walls) arranged in a plus shape, elevated above the ground. Because of the general aversion of mice to open spaces, mice tend to prefer the closed arms of the maze. The proportion of time spent in the open arms is therefore commonly used as a measure of anxiety-like behaviour: the more time spent in the open arms, the less anxious the mouse is.

Let's also provide credit to Loukia for sharing the data with us.

In this section we introduce the EPM paradigm and set up the analysis by importing the relevant libraries: `numpy`, `pandas`, `matplotlib`, `movement.sample_data`, `movement.filtering`, `movement.plots`, and `movement.roi`.

## Load and inspect the data

The EPM dataset is provided as part of `movement`'s built-in sample data and can be fetched with `sample_data.fetch_dataset("DLC_single-mouse_EPM.predictions.h5")`. Inspect the dataset structure.

## Clean the data

Raw pose-estimation output inevitably contains low-confidence or erroneous predictions, especially around occluded body parts. Here we use `movement.filtering.filter_by_confidence()` with a threshold of ~0.95 to discard unreliable predictions, and then apply a rolling median filter to smooth the remaining tracks. A similar pipeline was used in @sec-movement-intro, so no need to go into detail here, just apply the filtering operations (or could have the participants do it themselves as an exercise).

## Visualise space occupancy

Before performing any ROI-based analysis, it is useful to get a global impression of where the mouse spent its time. We use `movement.plots.plot_occupancy()` to generate a 2D histogram of the mouse's body centroid overlaid on the background frame, using a log-colour scale to reveal both high- and low-frequency regions.

Note that `movement.plot` provides some additional plotting functionality, on top of the built-in `xarray` methods we covered in @sec-movement-intro.

## Define ROIs in napari {#sec-epm-napari}

To formally separate the maze regions, we need to draw regions of interest (ROIs) as polygons in pixel coordinates. We do this interactively by launching the `movement` napari plugin, loading the background frame, adding an empty `Shapes` layer, and drawing five polygons—one for each maze region (left open arm, right open arm, bottom closed arm, top closed arm, and central square). Once drawn, the shapes are exported to a `.geojson` file.

Tell learners to launch napari and load the EPM video (show them where sample data is stored locally).
Cross-reference the napari section of precious chapter: @sec-movement-gui

For this part we could straight-up link to the [movement GUI guide](https://movement.neuroinformatics.dev/latest/user_guide/gui.html#define-regions-of-interest), as it already uses screenshots from the EPM example!

## Load and visualise ROIs

Load the exported `.geojson` file.

```{.python}
from movement.roi import load_rois

rois = load_rois("path/to/regions.geojson")
```

Explain briefly what the list of ROIs contains, and maybe visualise each ROI on top of the background frame using the region objects' `plot()` method. For reference, check out this [movement example](https://movement.neuroinformatics.dev/latest/examples/boundary_angles.html)

## Compute time spent in each ROI

With the ROIs defined, we use `movement.roi.compute_region_occupancy()` to determine, for each time point, which ROI (if any) contains the mouse's body centroid (computed as the mean position across all keypoints). The result is an `xarray.DataArray` of boolean values with a `region` dimension. Summing over time and expressing as a percentage of total frames yields the proportion of time spent in each maze region, which we could visualise as a bar chart (or export to a pandas DataFrame for further analysis).

Ideas for exercises:

How does the result change if you use a single keypoint (e.g. `tailbase` or `neck`) instead of the centroid of all keypoints to represent the mouse's position?

## Entries and exits (optional extension)

As an optional extension, we count the number of times the mouse enters and exits each ROI by detecting transitions in the boolean occupancy array. Entry/exit counts complement time-in-ROI as a measure of exploration and can reveal differences in behavioural strategy.
